fixes.explanation: Priests don't show up in this part of the story at all. The text says the believers shared everything they owned. When money comes in, it's laid at the apostles' feet for distribution to anyone as he had need. So the story points the money toward people with need, not toward the priests.

The temple doesn't show up here, friend. The text says the believers shared everything they owned, and the money was laid at the apostles' feet for distribution to anyone as he had need. A pile of stuff nobody touches sounds like the junk drawer I lived in for years. This crowd is doing the opposite.

The apostles are where the money gets laid, but the text says it was laid there "…for distribution to anyone as he had need." So "only the apostles" isn't what it says. The money is for anyone who has need. That's a wide-open door, friend.

Right, it's false. The text says "There were no needy ones among them…" The reason it gives is that those who owned lands or houses would sell their property and bring the proceeds. They laid the money at the apostles' feet for distribution to anyone as he had need (Acts 4:34-35). So the story says there were no needy ones among them.

Thunder is a loud name, friend, but it isn't this one. The text says Barnabas means Son of Encouragement. Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, gets that name from the apostles. Then it tells us he sold a field he owned, brought the money and laid it at the apostles' feet.

Peace is a lovely name, but it's not the one here. The text says Barnabas means Son of Encouragement. The apostles gave that name to Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus. I bet that's a name you'd want on your own apron.

That's right, baker. Barnabas sold a field he owned, brought the money and laid it at the apostles' feet. That's exactly the kind of giving the believers were doing. Remember this one, because the very next story comes right after it.
The text says otherwise, baker. Ananias kept back some of the proceeds "With his wife’s full knowledge…" So Sapphira knew he was keeping some back. She was in on what he was doing.
The text doesn't have Ananias going anywhere. On hearing Peter's words, he fell down and died. It's a heavy part of the story. I think it's one to read slowly.
You got it, baker. The text says great fear came over all who heard what had happened. That's the reaction it gives us. It's a heavy moment, and I think it's best to just let it be heavy.

It's true, friend. The text says Sapphira came in about three hours later, unaware of what had happened. Meanwhile the young men had already carried Ananias out and buried him (Acts 5:6). She walked in unaware.

That's what she says, baker. Peter asks, "is this the price you and your husband got for the land?" and Sapphira answers, "Yes," and says, "that is the price." It's the answer Peter responds to next. His very next words are, "How could you agree to test the Spirit of the Lord?"

Sapphira doesn't say that, baker. When Peter asks if this is the price she and her husband got for the land, she answers, "Yes," and says, "that is the price." She doesn't mention asking anybody. That answer is what Peter responds to next.

Honor is the opposite of what Peter says, friend. His words are, "How could you agree to test the Spirit of the Lord?" Honoring the Spirit and testing the Spirit are two very different things. I think Peter's question is a heavy one, and the word he picks is test.

Follow is a good word, baker, but it isn't Peter's. He asks, "How could you agree to test the Spirit of the Lord?" Following would be walking behind the Spirit, and testing is something else. The word in the text is test.
The text doesn't say where that burial place was, baker. The young men carried her out and buried her beside her husband. That's the detail it gives us. Nothing else is added about the spot.
